bivy.name: The US 2 pullout by the maintenance yard
bivy.capacity: Shoulder parking and a pullout by the road turnoff for the maintenance station, with room for about three vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground, no fee site, no table and no toilet. In winter the plough berm decides how much of it exists on any given morning.
bivy.water: Nason Creek runs alongside and under the highway bridge the route crosses, and it needs treating. There is no potable supply. THERE IS NO WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN ITSELF once you leave the creek and the lower spur — the north ridge and the clearcut above carry nothing, so in summer everything is carried from here, and in winter the answer is melting snow.
bivy.permit: None. This is not designated wilderness, there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no lottery anywhere on this peak. Highway shoulder parking needs no forest pass, which is worth knowing because the trailheads a few miles either side of it do. There is no fee and no registration. Note that the WSDOT rest area further along the highway is a rest area and not a campground, and overnight camping there is not what it is for.
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead and, realistically, the accommodation. The pullout sits roughly seven miles east of Stevens Pass at the east tunnel end. The route walks west along the highway shoulder for a few hundred yards, crosses the Nason Creek bridge and drops onto an old logging spur that parallels the creek to the railway grade; parties then follow the tracks a short way before scrambling up the bank at about 2,700 ft and climbing steep timber to snowline around 3,700 ft. A variation stays on the spur, crosses Henry Creek, takes the right fork and then the left to the bottom of a clearcut at about 4,200 ft, climbs the clearcut directly south and traverses east into the trees to gain the north ridge. TWO CAUTIONS THAT ARE NOT ABOUT CLIMBING. The highway shoulder walk is on a fast, busy road with poor sightlines and is more dangerous than anything above it, and the railway line is active — treat both as hazards to be got off quickly rather than as part of the walk. Winter parking here is genuinely tight and the shoulder is where the ploughs put the snow, so an early arrival is worth more than an early start.

bivy.name: The clearcut benches on the north ridge, around 4,200 feet
bivy.capacity: No established site of any kind. Under deep snow the clearcut and the flat bench above it give as much room as a party wants; in bare conditions there is very little usable flat ground and it is all slash, stumps and brush. Recorded to say plainly that nobody camps on this mountain, rather than to invent a site for it.
bivy.water: None whatsoever. Henry Creek on the lower spur is the last water on the way up and it is a long way below. In winter this is a snow camp and you melt; in summer you carry, and the amount you would have to carry is the argument against being here at all.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness national forest and old logging ground, no permit, no quota, no fee. Fires are a poor idea in a clearcut full of dry slash and are prohibited under the summer restrictions that run most years on this side of the pass. Some of the lower spur network crosses a mix of ownership, so read the signs at the junctions rather than assuming everything is public.
bivy.notes: Included as a contingency and as an honest negative. There is no reason to sleep on Arrowhead: the whole outing is six miles and three thousand feet and a fit party is up and down in seven or eight hours, so the only situation where this ground matters is a winter party that has broken trail through deep new snow, run out of daylight low down, and would rather bivouac than descend a steep wooded slope in the dark. Under those conditions the flat around the top of the clearcut at roughly 4,200 ft is the obvious place, being out of the timber and out of the terrain trap of the creek drainages. What you get is a snow camp with no shelter and no water; what you avoid is a night descent. In summer this same ground is slash and regrowth and there is nothing to recommend it. THE ROUTE IS CHOSEN FOR ITS AVALANCHE CHARACTER and is described as steep but safe by that measure, which is exactly the sort of judgement that changes with the year's snowpack — assess it rather than inheriting it.

bivy.name: Tumwater Canyon campgrounds on US 2
bivy.capacity: Small developed forest campgrounds strung along the highway in the canyon between Leavenworth and the Chiwaukum front, taking modest vehicles and a moderate number of parties. Sites are a mix of first come and reservable, and they fill on summer weekends with Leavenworth traffic that has nothing to do with the mountains.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed sites during the operating season, plus the river alongside. This is the one place in this file where water is not a problem, and it is the sensible place to fill everything before driving up to the pullout.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee at the developed campgrounds, with some sites reservable in advance and the rest first come, first served. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply through the summer in the canyon and are commonly total bans by late season — this is one of the driest and most fire-prone stretches of highway in the state.
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in camping to Arrowhead that is not already recorded in a neighbouring zone file, deliberately chosen over the Lake Wenatchee corridor camps for that reason. It is a drive of half an hour or so west along the highway to the pullout, which suits a party that wants a proper night with water and a table before a dawn start. The catch is the season: these canyon campgrounds run roughly late spring to early autumn, which is precisely the half of the year when Arrowhead is at its worst. FOR THE WINTER ASCENT, WHICH IS THE ONE MOST PARTIES WANT, THESE ARE CLOSED and the answer is a night in the vehicle at the pullout or a very early drive from town. Note also that the December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this district and a closure order covering them runs into 2027, and that a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026; neither touches the highway itself, but both change what is open either side of it, so check before relying on a specific campground.

bivy.name: The lower spur and Henry Creek flat
bivy.capacity: Rough ground on the old logging road network in the first mile, where the spur crosses Henry Creek. Room for a tent or two on the road grade itself. Nothing established, nothing signed, and no reason to be here except timing.
bivy.water: Henry Creek at the crossing, and Nason Creek below — both need treating and both run all year. This is the last water on the route and the only water on it, and its position at the very bottom of the climb is the whole water story of this peak: everything above is dry, so this is where you fill.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness, no permit, no quota. The spur network crosses mixed ownership in places, including railway and utility corridors, so read the signage at junctions and do not assume a road is open ground just because it is drivable-looking. No fee, no registration.
bivy.notes: Recorded chiefly as the water point rather than as a camp, because knowing where Henry Creek is matters more on this mountain than knowing where you could pitch. The spur climbs east-southeast off the highway after the Nason Creek bridge, crosses the creek, and then forks twice — right at the first junction by an unnamed creek, left at the second — before reaching the bottom of the clearcut at about 4,200 ft. In winter the fork-finding is the navigational crux of the day and it is done under snow with the road cuts filled in, which is why parties who have been up before make much better time than parties who have not. As sleeping ground it is a poor substitute for the pullout, being no warmer, no flatter and a mile further from the car, and its one genuine use is for a party arriving in the small hours who would rather walk a mile and sleep than sit on the highway shoulder. Bring an axe for the steep timber above regardless of season; the slope from the railway grade to snowline is unrelenting.

bivy.name: Chiwaukum Chain Lakes
bivy.capacity: Numerous informal sites spread around the three lakes, on benches and in the timber edges. There is room for several parties and you will rarely be competing for ground — the walk in is long enough from either end that this basin stays quiet even in high summer.
bivy.water: Excellent and the reason this is the camp. All three lakes hold water through the season, the inlet streams run well into late summer, and the basin is the last dependable supply before the scramble. Everything above the lakes is dry once the snow has gone, so fill completely here for summit day. Treat it; the shoreline sees steady if light use.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register and covers both day and overnight use; there is no quota, no reservation and no lottery on this side of the wilderness, which is the opposite of the Enchantments permit zone a few miles south. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the Icicle Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this wilderness, which includes every lake in this basin — carry a stove. Party size is capped, camp on existing bare ground and keep well back from the lakeshores.
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Bulls Tooth and the only place a party should plan to sleep for the standard scramble. From the upper lake the route works around the shore to the base of a northwest-facing couloir filled with big white talus, climbs that to the ridge, and finishes on the summit block; most parties rappel the top section on the way down rather than reversing it, so a rope and a small rack of slings for the anchors belongs on the list even though the outing is graded as a scramble. Reaching the basin from the Icicle side is about two and a half miles and two thousand feet of climbing off the Icicle Creek trail on the Chain Lakes trail, which itself is roughly five miles and nineteen hundred feet from the junction — a full day with an overnight load. That trail was destroyed by a landslide a couple of miles south of Lake Josephine and has never been rebuilt to its old standard: it is passable on foot, it is not recommended for stock, and it is slow and vague where the slide crossed. From the west the basin is reached over Frosty Pass instead. Snow lingers in these basins into July in a normal year and the couloir holds it longer, which suits a party carrying an axe and hurts one that is not.

bivy.name: Doelle Lakes
bivy.capacity: Flat camping in alpine meadow threaded with talus, with room for several parties spread out. Genuinely lightly used — most people who reach the Chain Lakes stop there.
bivy.water: Both lakes, reliable through the climbing season, plus snowmelt in the talus early. This is the other dependable supply in the group and the one to use if the Chain Lakes basin is occupied.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the trailhead register, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass at the Icicle Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 5,000 feet, and at this elevation the ground is thin subalpine meadow that scars for years, so pitch on bare gravel or existing sites and use a stove.
bivy.notes: About one and eight tenths miles and six hundred feet above the Chain Lakes, this is the higher and more scenic option and it looks straight across at Bulls Tooth, which is the highest thing in view from here. It is the natural camp for a party that is traversing rather than going in and out — the usual line runs Icicle Creek to the Chain Lakes, over to Doelle, out past Bulls Tooth to Frosty Pass and down Wildhorse Creek to Whitepine, and this basin is the middle of it. As a base for the scramble alone it is slightly further from the couloir than the Chain Lakes are, so parties climbing the peak and returning the same way usually stay lower. The meadows here are exposed and hold weather; there is very little shelter and nights are cold well into August at this height. The connecting ground between here and the Chain Lakes is open enough to be simple in clear weather and genuinely confusing in cloud.

bivy.name: Frosty Pass and the Wildhorse Creek headwaters
bivy.capacity: Established ground at and just below the pass for a couple of parties, with more scattered spots in the meadows on the Wildhorse side. A crossroads rather than a destination, so expect the occasional through party in July and August and nobody at all in September.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small streams in the headwater meadows below the pass on the Wildhorse side, dependable into midsummer and thinning badly by late season. The pass itself carries nothing you can rely on. This is the last water on the western approach before the high ground, and the Icicle Ridge trail east of here is notoriously dry, so fill in the meadows rather than at the crest.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the White Pine trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet — this camp is above that line and there is very little to burn regardless. Camp on the existing bare sites; the meadow here is fragile and heavily walked.
bivy.notes: This is the pivot of the western approach to Bulls Tooth and the last camp before the peak from that side. The Frosty and Wildhorse Creek trail runs about eleven miles and thirty-five hundred feet from the Whitepine side to the pass, where it meets the Icicle Ridge trail; from the pass the high country opens out east and north toward Lake Grace, Snowgrass Mountain, the Doelle Lakes and Bulls Tooth itself. THE TRAIL IS NOT MAINTAINED BEYOND THE PASS, so the ground linking this camp to the peak is route-finding on open high country rather than trail walking, and it is the part of the trip most likely to go wrong in poor visibility. Lake Grace lies off to the side and is the better camp of the two if you want water you can count on and shelter from the wind, at the cost of some distance. Parties doing the full traverse come over this pass in either direction, and it works as well for a party who has climbed the peak from the Chain Lakes and is walking out west as it does for one coming in. Season is roughly mid-July through early October; the north-facing approach slopes hold snow late and the pass is a cold, exposed place to be caught out.

bivy.name: Whitepine Creek valley camps and the Wildhorse junction ford
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the first few miles of the Whitepine Creek trail, most taking one or two tents, each with its own bit of creek. Nothing developed and no toilets.
bivy.water: Whitepine Creek runs alongside for the whole of this stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous part of the approach, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Frosty Pass and everything above it is a different story.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the White Pine trailhead register. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below 5,000 feet in existing rings outside a burn ban, but this is dry east-side timber and the district runs restrictions through most of the summer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk, and on an approach this long that matters more than it sounds. It is roughly three miles of easy valley trail from the road end to the Wildhorse Creek junction, and then six and a half miles of climbing to Frosty Pass — a poor single day with a loaded pack after the drive out from the west side. THE CRUX OF THE WHOLE APPROACH IS THE WHITEPINE CREEK FORD, a few hundred yards short of the Wildhorse junction near the ruins of the old bridge. Early in the season with snowmelt running it is a serious crossing and it is the thing that turns parties round; by late July or August it is usually a boots-on wade with a stick. Camping short of it and crossing in the morning, when the flow is at its lowest and you are fresh, is the standard tactic and the right one. Coming out, most parties walk straight through. The valley is forested and pleasant and the walking is fast, which is the argument for the Whitepine approach over the Icicle one whenever the Icicle road or the French Creek bridge is out.

bivy.name: White Pine road end trailhead
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the end of the road with room for a modest number of vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground here, no facilities and no fee site — this is a roadhead, recorded because a party arriving late from the west side needs somewhere to be.
bivy.water: Whitepine Creek is at hand and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill everything here before starting, since the good water lasts only as far as the valley and the high country above Frosty Pass has almost none.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is taken from the register here rather than arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Fire restrictions on this dry east slope are close to permanent through the summer and commonly ban all open flame including in rings.
bivy.notes: The staging point for the western approach and the shorter drive from anywhere on US 2. The road leaves the highway west of Leavenworth and runs about four miles of gravel to the trailhead at roughly 2,800 feet. Sleeping here rather than pushing into the valley in the dark is worth doing, because the ford above wants daylight and a party that arrives at it tired in the evening will camp short of it anyway. THE ROAD IS THE PART TO CHECK. The December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this whole district and a closure order covering the damaged ones runs into 2027; the Icicle road on the other side of the range carries multiple landslides limiting vehicles to the end of the road, and a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026, shutting more than sixty trails in these two districts. Confirm the White Pine road and the Whitepine and Wildhorse trails are open before committing to the drive, and have the Icicle side as a fallback rather than an assumption, because in some seasons it has been the worse of the two.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. Sources differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.
bivy.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
bivy.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.

bivy.name: Pelton Basin
bivy.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.
bivy.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day. No elevation is recorded because no confident figure was sourced.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.

bivy.capacity: A highway pullout and viewpoint parking area, not a campground. Parties routinely spend the night in a vehicle here to start at first light. There are no sites, no pitches, and nowhere to put a tent.
bivy.water: Gorge Creek itself, immediately below, and it is the last certain water for a long way up. Nothing is provided at the pullout.
bivy.permit: No permit and no fee to park or to sleep in a vehicle. A DAY climb from here needs no backcountry permit at all, which is the usual way this peak is done. The moment you sleep on the mountain you need a National Park Service backcountry permit for the Davis Peak cross-country zone.
bivy.notes: This is where the standard scramble starts, on Highway 20 between Newhalem and Diablo. You cross the creek on the bridge and go straight into steep forest with no trail of any kind. The peak is famous for the sheer drop off its far side, and the ground you climb reflects that: expect around ten miles and roughly seven and a half thousand feet of gain, with cliff bands to be turned in the timber around twenty-four hundred and twenty-eight hundred feet and a stretch of vine maple higher. Thirteen or fourteen hours car to car is a normal time for a fit party, and that is why so many sleep at the car rather than carry overnight gear up it. Being west of the seasonal highway gate, the pullout is reachable all year, but the route wants firm snow or dry ground rather than the rotten mix in between.

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, Newhalem
bivy.capacity: A modest road campground on the Skagit with a mix of standard sites and a couple of group sites, small enough that a busy summer weekend fills it.
bivy.water: Potable water while the campground is serviced; the river is the fallback and needs treating. Availability drops off outside the main season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No backcountry permit needed to sleep here. It has historically been the free, year-round, minimal-service option in the Newhalem cluster while the fee campgrounds close for winter — confirm the current fee and season, because the park has been adjusting both.
bivy.notes: About five minutes' drive west of the Gorge Creek overlook, this is the practical base for a party that wants a real campsite the night before rather than a night in the driver's seat. It is low, forested and close to the highway, with none of the character of the alpine above it, and that is fine for its purpose. It also stays open later in the year than the larger campgrounds nearby, which matters on a peak whose best conditions are often outside the busy season. THE OBVIOUS CLOSER OPTION IS GONE: the small tent campground at Gorge Lake, right beside the creek in Diablo, has been shut for an extended period over debris-flow and flooding hazard on ground burned in an earlier fire, and should not be planned around without confirming it has reopened.

bivy.name: Snowfield benches on the south side, around 4,800 feet
bivy.capacity: Open ground rather than sites. Where the timber finally releases into alpine snow and slabs there is room for a small party to lie down, and no established platform to aim for.
bivy.water: Running snowmelt while there is snow, which is exactly what makes this level worth stopping at. Once the slopes bare out later in summer, water here becomes unreliable and the gully lower down is the last dependable source.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Davis Peak cross-country zone: six people maximum in a party, and a maximum of three parties in the zone on any night. Walk-up only, collected in person at the Marblemount wilderness office rather than reserved in advance. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and not in meadow or within a hundred feet of water. No fires anywhere in the zone. Pack waste out where the ground will not take a cathole.
bivy.notes: The forest below is the whole difficulty of this mountain — steep, tangled and unrelenting, with the route picked out along animal paths and through weaknesses in the cliff bands. Getting up to this level and stopping turns a punishing single day into a manageable two, and this is the first ground on the route where a party can lie flat and see out. A partly snow-filled gully around four thousand feet is the usual way through the last of the trees onto these slopes; it is straightforward when it holds firm snow and considerably less pleasant when it is running wet or bare. Early summer is the moment for this camp, because the same snow that makes the gully work is what supplies the water.

bivy.name: The 5,720 ft saddle south of the summit
bivy.capacity: Room for about two small tents on a snow ledge by the saddle. That is the whole capacity, and it is not a place to plan on sharing.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only while snow is present at the notch. Late in a dry summer there is nothing here and everything has to be carried up from the snowfields below.
bivy.permit: Same National Park Service backcountry permit and Davis Peak cross-country zone as the ground below: party of six maximum, three parties per night, walk-up from Marblemount, no fires, durable surfaces only.
bivy.notes: A little over half a mile south of the summit, this notch in the ridge is the highest sensible sleeping ground on the peak and the launching point for the last of the climbing. From here the standard finish takes the rock buttress on the south ridge at easy scrambling, a couple of grades of hands-on ground rather than anything technical. Parties have also tried the broad snow slopes of the east ridge from the saddle and been stopped by a step a few hundred feet under the top, so the south side is the line to plan for. Being a saddle it is exposed to whatever the weather is doing and there is nothing to shelter behind, which argues for using it on a settled forecast and otherwise sleeping lower. NOTE THE OTHER APPROACH: the peak's steep north-east side is reached instead from the Stetattle Creek trail out of Diablo, leaving the path after a couple of miles and fording the creek — but that trail has been closed outright for falling dead trees on burned ground, so treat the Gorge Creek side as the only way in until it reopens.

bivy.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots only, with a hard limit of FOUR people on the site. That is the smallest party cap of anything on this approach and it rules the camp out for a larger group entirely.
bivy.water: Sourdough Creek runs at the camp and is the first water on the whole climb from Diablo — the lower trail has essentially none. Early in the season the crossing can be bridged by snow, which is worth treating with care rather than walking onto.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, collected at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing process. This is a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night rather than open ground, so a walk-up can be refused. A BEAR CANISTER IS REQUIRED here through the main season; the park lends them free at the permit desk. No fires. Pets are not allowed at the camp.
bivy.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first three and a half miles are relentless forest switchbacks with nothing to drink. Stopping here makes the second day the good one. Note that the climbers' line for Elephant Butte does not continue to the lookout at all — it leaves this trail at an unmarked junction somewhere around four thousand three hundred to four thousand four hundred feet and turns north up the ridge crest west of the creek. No elevation is recorded for the camp because no confident figure was found. Both this camp and the trail it sits on have been closed by fire for most of the last three years; confirm before planning around it.

bivy.name: Pierce Mountain Camp
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp set among tarns, with the same limit of FOUR people. Assigned by night on the permit.
bivy.water: The tarns beside the camp, and they are the only dependable supply on that whole upper stretch. They are shallow standing pools, so treat what you take.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. A bear canister is required here through the main season, as at Sourdough Camp. No fires.
bivy.notes: About a mile east of the lookout, on the seldom-used trail that runs out along the ridge toward Ross Lake. Its value to this peak is as the other way in: a party can reach the same ridge system from the Ross Dam trailhead further east on Highway 20, going the long way around Sourdough Mountain, and that is exactly what a recent traverse did when the Sourdough trail was closed by fire. It is brushy and overgrown low down and adds distance, so nobody chooses it while the direct trail is open. The lookout itself is closed to the public and is not somewhere to sleep. No elevation is recorded because the figures found for it were not confirmable.

bivy.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country ground rather than sites. Small grassy pockets and gravel benches recur the length of the ridge, easily enough for the zone's limit of six parties, and no two accounts stop in the same place.
bivy.water: Small tarns and snowmelt ponds scattered over the ridge — plentiful in late June, and the single best reason to come early. THEY DO DRY. By August in a warm year parties report water on the ridge becoming a real problem, and which pools survive latest is not documented anywhere reliable. Late in the season carry enough to camp dry.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. There is NO Stetattle Ridge zone — the ridge falls between the Sourdough zone and the Elephant Butte zone, and your permit has to name the one you will actually sleep in. Both allow a party of six and six parties a night. Neither is reservable in advance: they are walk-up zones, issued in person, with a share of the allocation held for same-day and next-day pickup. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow pockets that make the ridge look inviting, and not within a hundred feet of a tarn. NO FIRES in a cross-country zone. Waste in a cathole, or carried out on snow and bare rock. A canister is not formally required in these two zones, but the ridge is open ground with nothing to hang from, so bring one anyway.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went for the summit from there. It is still a long way: from the ridge high point the ground drops something like fifteen hundred feet before you regain that and another thousand to the top, and a full trip is closer to twenty miles and ten thousand feet of gain and loss over two nights. Several strong parties have reached the ridge in a single push and turned round because the butte was still too far. The north-east side of the crest is very steep, so stay on it or just south-west of it. Snow-free is roughly late July into September, which is unhelpfully the same window in which the water disappears.

bivy.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
bivy.capacity: Open ground near the summit, a small party at a time. In winter and spring it is a snow camp with no defined pitch at all.
bivy.water: Melted snow in the cold months, which is when this site makes sense. In summer there is nothing at the summit and the tarns further along the ridge are the supply.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Sourdough cross-country zone: six people per party, six parties a night, walk-up only. The lookout building is closed and camping is not permitted at it, so the site is the open ground near the top rather than the structure. Same durable-surface, no-fire and no-meadow rules as the rest of the zone.
bivy.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in the corridor reachable in winter — a late-March overnight on continuous snow is a known way to do the ridge, with the caveat that spring sun softens the slopes badly by mid-morning. For a summer ascent of the butte it is a detour, since the climbers' line leaves the trail well below the lookout and never comes here. It also carries the same warning as everything else in this file: the trail, both designated camps, and the Sourdough and Elephant Butte zones have all been closed by an active fire in the drainage, on top of an earlier fire that shut the trail for two and a half years before it briefly reopened. Check the closure status first; it is the single thing most likely to end this trip.

bivy.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
bivy.capacity: No established site and no name. Parties travelling the crest report finding flat ground on the shoulder and on the benches near the pass east of the peak, tight enough that three tents felt crowded. Treat it as somewhere you stop, not somewhere you book.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small pools, entirely seasonal. There is no dependable source and nothing to plan on. Fill on the ridge before committing to the descent toward the butte.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Elephant Butte cross-country zone: six people maximum, six parties a night, walk-up only from Marblemount. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail and out of sight of both, which up here is automatic. Durable surfaces only, no fires, waste packed out above treeline.
bivy.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at walking-to-scrambling ground. The EAST ridge is a different proposition entirely and has been described by a party crossing it on a long Picket traverse as among the hardest ground of that whole trip, needing roped downclimbs and rappels — so do not read the easy summit as an easy mountain from every side. The named benches near the pass east of the butte belong to the traverse route rather than to this approach, and a party coming from Stetattle Ridge will not pass them. NO ELEVATION IS RECORDED: no account that slept on this shoulder coming from Stetattle Ridge stated one, and the figures published for the traverse-side benches describe different ground.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.

Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and several accounts describe that decision being regretted around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.

bivy.name: Massie Lake basin
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake for one or two parties. There is nothing developed, nothing signed and no toilet, and the basin is small — but it is also so little visited that competition for space is not a realistic worry.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable all season. This is the last certain water on the climb and the reason to camp here rather than higher: the slopes and benches above the basin run on snowmelt only and are dry by August in an ordinary year. Fill completely before going up. Treat it, though the shoreline sees very little use.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the Trinity trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book in advance. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at Trinity. Camp back from the shoreline and on existing bare ground; this is a small basin and it marks easily. Carry a stove — summer fire restrictions on this dry east side are routine and often total.
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Massie Peak and effectively the only one, because everything above it is dry and everything below it is a long way down. From the Trinity trailhead the Buck Creek trail runs a mile and a half to the junction, the Chiwawa River trail carries on up the valley and crosses the river on a bridge, and about three miles along it the Massie Lake trail turns off and climbs roughly two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake. THAT LAST STRETCH IS THE DIFFICULTY AND IT IS NOT A TRAIL IN ANY USEFUL SENSE. It is an unsigned and unmaintained old sheep driveway, steep, brushy and lost altogether in places, and the standard complaint about this lake is the amount of bushwhacking involved in reaching it. Expect to lose the line more than once and to be pushing through vegetation on the steepest part of the day. From camp the west route on Massie Peak goes on open slopes above the basin and is a scramble rather than a climb. The reward for the thrash is genuine solitude and good fishing; the register-level traffic here is a fraction of what the Buck Creek Pass side sees. Season is roughly mid-July into early October, later than a lake this height would suggest because the brush is at its worst when it is wet.

bivy.name: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the timber along the valley floor, including good ground where the trail crosses the river on the bridge. One or two parties each, nothing developed, and rarely anyone else there.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is alongside for this whole stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is where the approach is generous with water, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Massie Lake is the steep, hot, brushy part and there is nothing dependable on it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit from the Trinity trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below the high country in existing rings outside a burn ban, but the Chiwawa valley is dry and bans are the norm from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.notes: These are the first-night camps for a party that has driven a long way, or the last-night camps for one walking out, and on this approach both cases are common. The river bridge where the Buck Creek trail crosses is the usual spot and is the obvious place to stop, being flat, sheltered and on good water. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the Massie Lake turn is unsigned and the driveway above it is steep and vague — that is ground you want to meet in the morning with fresh legs and a full day, not at dusk. The valley walking below is gentle and fast, so a party that gets away from the road in the afternoon can be here comfortably. THE ROAD CLOSURE CHANGES THE ARITHMETIC ENTIRELY. With the Chiwawa River road shut above Atkinson Flat, Trinity is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns the walk to these camps into a long day on its own or a bike shuttle, and turns the trip as a whole from two nights into three or four.

bivy.name: Trinity trailhead roadhead
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the end of the public road with room to sleep in a vehicle. It is a roadhead, not a campground — no fee site, no tables, no toilet you should count on. The developed campgrounds strung along the Chiwawa River road below it are the proper drive-in option and are recorded in the Entiat and Holden file rather than repeated here.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is close by and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap anywhere at this end of the road. Fill everything here, since the valley trail above is good for water and the climb to the lake is not.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is taken from the register here — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit including stock. Fire restrictions bite hard on this side from midsummer and commonly ban all open flame including in existing rings.
bivy.notes: The staging point, and it is recorded because the drive is the part of this trip that most often goes wrong. In a normal year the Chiwawa River road runs about twenty-two miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, with the last stretch rough gravel genuinely unsuited to low clearance, and arriving at the end of it late and tired is how parties end up starting the walk in badly. From the roadhead a short section of closed road leads onto the Buck Creek trail, and the junction where the Chiwawa River trail branches right for Massie is a mile and a half in. THE ROAD IS SHUT ABOVE ATKINSON FLAT under a storm-damage order running into 2027, with the 2026 fire closure sitting over the same corridor on top of it, and while that stands there is no legal way to drive to this roadhead at all. When the road is open again, expect it to remain the fragile part of any plan here: it has been damaged repeatedly, it carries no through traffic to justify quick repair, and the trailhead is far enough up it that a single washout removes the whole approach.

bivy.name: The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
bivy.capacity: None established. There is open ground on the benches and in the meadows above the lake where a small party could put down a tent, but nothing has been built, nothing is marked, and nobody camps here as a matter of course. This entry exists to say so plainly rather than to invent a site.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. By August there is usually nothing at all above the lake, and a party sleeping up here is carrying every drop from the basin below. This is the single most common way to get the trip wrong.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at Trinity. No fires this high — carry a stove. The ground is thin subalpine turf that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.notes: Recorded honestly: Massie Peak is a day objective from the lake and there is no practical reason to sleep higher. The scramble from the basin is short enough that the only argument for going up is to be on the crest at first light, and the cost is carrying water two thousand feet and sleeping exposed with nothing to shelter behind. The one situation where these benches genuinely earn their place is the traverse northwest on the old sheepherder's line toward Pass No Pass and the Buck Creek Pass country, which runs two and a half to three miles on faint stock and game tracks that come and go, and which a party will not finish in the same day they climb the peak. If you are doing that, sleeping high on the way out makes sense. If you are climbing Massie and walking back down the driveway, it does not. Either way, do not plan on finding water and do not plan on finding a flat, cleared spot.

bivy.name: Airplane Lake
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on benches around the lake for one or two parties. Nothing developed, nothing signed, no toilet — and almost certainly nobody else there. This is a genuinely lightly visited basin and solitude is the main thing it offers.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the climbing season along with snowmelt into the inlet early on. This is the last certain water on the mountain: the two thousand feet of slope between the lake and the summit carry nothing once the snow has gone. Fill everything here for the climb and for the night, and treat it.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the White River trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at the trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground; the basin is small. Carry a stove — the district runs summer fire restrictions on this dry east side as a matter of course and they are often total bans.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Mount Saul and effectively the only one, and camping here is what turns a brutal outing into a reasonable two days. Done in a single push from the road the standard route runs about sixteen miles round trip with five thousand three hundred feet of gain, which is a long day by any measure and a very long one on ground this rough. The lake sits roughly two thousand two hundred feet above Indian Creek, in a large depression under the upper east slopes, with the summit still some two thousand feet above it — so a party sleeping here has the worst of the climbing behind them and a clean morning on the east slope and east face. THE APPROACH PATH IS THE HARD PART. It leaves the Indian Creek trail at about four and a half miles, immediately before a valley campsite, marked only by a sign stating that marking of routes is prohibited; there is no other signage and the track is faint. It climbs steeply through the 2016 burn, which means loose footing, no shade, blowdown that changes with every windstorm and standing dead timber overhead. Recent volunteer work has had the trail in good condition in places, but that is a season-by-season matter rather than a promise. Season is roughly mid-July into early October; the east side melts out reasonably early but the upper slopes hold snow and an axe is worth carrying in the first half of the summer.

bivy.name: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the Indian Creek trail, one or two tents each, including the established spot immediately past the unsigned turn for Airplane Lake. Nothing developed and no facilities.
bivy.water: Indian Creek runs beside the trail for the whole of this stretch and water is abundant; parts of the valley trail are boggy in early season for the same reason. Every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous half of the approach and it ends the moment you start climbing.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal in existing rings at this elevation outside a burn ban, but bans are usual here from midsummer and much of the surrounding forest is fire-killed, so use a stove.
bivy.notes: The junction camp is the useful one and it is the landmark as much as the site: the climbers' path for Airplane Lake turns off immediately before it, so a party that reaches an obvious valley campsite and has seen no turning has just walked past the only one there is. Sleeping here rather than at the lake trades a shorter, easier first day for a much harder second one, and most parties would rather push to the lake. Where it earns its place is on the way out, and for a party that has been slowed by the road or the burn and does not want to start the two-thousand-foot climbers' path in the evening. The valley trail itself runs about ten and a half miles in total to the Pacific Crest Trail at Indian Pass, crossing the White River on a bridge right at the trailhead and then climbing very gently; it is brushy and boggy in places, which is a nuisance rather than an obstacle. Expect burn for long stretches, and treat the dead timber overhead as a real reason not to pitch under it in wind.

bivy.name: White River road end trailhead
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the road end with room to sleep in a vehicle, and no campground facilities. This is a roadhead recorded because a party arriving from the west side in the evening needs somewhere to be before starting an approach this long.
bivy.water: The White River is at the trailhead and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill here, and fill again from Indian Creek on the way up, because everything above the valley is dry.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit comes from the register here rather than being arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit. Fire restrictions on this side are near-permanent through summer and commonly ban open flame entirely.
bivy.notes: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. THE ROAD IS THE FRAGILE PART AND HAS BEEN CLOSED TWICE IN ONE SEASON. It is named in the storm-damage closure order following the December 2025 floods, which runs into 2027 with no reopening estimate, and it sat inside the summer 2026 fire closure across the Wenatchee River and Entiat districts as well. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.

bivy.name: The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
bivy.capacity: None established. There is broken ground and the occasional flat spot on the slope between the lake and the summit rocks where a small party could put a tent down, but nothing has been built and nobody camps here as a matter of course. Recorded so the absence is stated rather than filled in with an invented site.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. From roughly August onward there is nothing at all above the lake, and anyone sleeping here carries every drop up two thousand feet. This is the mistake to avoid rather than a plan to make.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the White River trailhead. No fires at this elevation and nothing to burn. The ground is thin alpine turf and scree that scars for years — camp on rock or gravel if you camp at all.
bivy.notes: The honest answer for this peak is that Airplane Lake is the camp and there is nothing above it worth having. The lake already puts the summit within a straightforward morning on the east slope and east face, so climbing higher with a pack buys almost nothing and costs the water, the shelter and the flat ground all at once. The northwest face is sheer and is not the way anyone goes; the east side is open scrambling terrain and the difficulty of this mountain lies in the approach rather than in the climbing. Where a high bivouac has any argument at all is for a party linking Saul with the ridge country toward Indian Head and the crest, which is a different and much longer trip, and even then the sensible pattern is to sleep at water and move over the tops in the day. Treat anything above the lake as emergency ground.

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff. No elevation is recorded because no confident figure was sourced.

bivy.name: Beaver Pass Camp
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites
bivy.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the source, and there are no facilities of any kind.

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.

bivy.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
bivy.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit
bivy.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water anywhere in this file. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
bivy.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph.
