Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
bivy.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.

bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover
bivy.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench
bivy.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
bivy.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers rather than deciding from a guidebook. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.capacity: Very limited, realistically two to four small tents; parties have ended up stacking tents in a vertical line on the slope when the site is busy, which is not a safe arrangement
bivy.water: Snow only. There is no water and no shelter, so carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively only bivouac on Liberty Ridge, a notch of snow and rock partway up the ridge on the Carbon Glacier side. It is exposed to rockfall from Thumb Rock itself and from the bands above, and a fatal rockfall struck tents here in 2019, so site selection within the notch and the timing of your arrival matter more than comfort. Warm afternoons that prevent an overnight freeze are the usual trigger, and the park service advises against the route when the freezing level on the mountain is high. The approach from the Carbon River or Mowich side is long and its own seasonal problem, since those roads open on different schedules and can be closed by washouts or fire.

bivy.name: White River Campground
bivy.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
bivy.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.capacity: 179 individual sites across six loops, plus separate group sites
bivy.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park entrance applies, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up on summit morning. Campsites are reservable through Recreation.gov and required during the peak midsummer window. This covers the campground only and is unrelated to the wilderness permit and climbing fee.
bivy.notes: Between Longmire and Paradise on the southwest side, the practical roadhead camp for anything staging out of Paradise — Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar. Because the Nisqually entrance road is kept open through the year, it is the least season-gated approach on the mountain, though the campground itself runs roughly late May to late September. It sits low and forested at just over 3,000 ft, which makes for comfortable sleeping but no acclimatisation value whatsoever. Book early, since it is one of only two campgrounds in the park taking reservations and fills on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.

bivy.name: Dolly Varden Camp, upper Stehekin valley road
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp beside the old road, a handful of sites in forest by the river. Assigned by night on the permit.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River is immediately there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river and carries silt as well as everything else in the drainage.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Obtained at the Golden West visitor centre at the landing on arrival, or at Marblemount if you are coming over a pass. THE PERMIT AND THE BOAT HAVE TO AGREE: an itinerary that slips a day because you missed a sailing needs the permit amended, and the office that can do that is back at the landing.
bivy.notes: About thirteen miles up from the landing, which puts it roughly two above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge. Its whole purpose on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day, the last shuttle up the valley leaves in the late afternoon, and nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on that schedule — so you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way, and sleep. It is flat forest with no view and no alpine character at all, which is exactly what it is for. NOTE ANOTHER CLOSURE NEARBY: the camp at Tumwater, at around two thousand feet a little further down the same stretch of road, has been shut after high water damaged it, and the park asked people to stay away from the valley altogether after a bad flood. Between that and the fire seasons, confirm which upper-valley camps are actually open before you build the itinerary, because there are not many of them and losing one changes the whole plan.

bivy.name: Flat Creek Camp, at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: A physically large camp that nonetheless takes only about two large groups, so it is emptier than it looks and still bookable out. Stock parties use it as well as walkers.
bivy.water: Flat Creek runs at the camp and the Stehekin River is close by. Both are reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, same system as the rest of the valley. This camp sits inside the park; the ground you climb on does not. See the note below on where the boundary falls, because the two agencies want different things and the changeover happens two miles up the trail.
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE CAMP FOR THE PEAK. It sits where the Flat Creek trail leaves the old valley road, about nine and a half miles above High Bridge on what used to be driveable and has been a walking route since the river took the road out for the last time more than two decades ago. That distance is the real cost of this objective: the public shuttle stops at High Bridge and everything above it is on foot, so from the boat you are looking at twenty miles of approach before the climbing starts. From here the Flat Creek trail runs four miles or so up the valley on gentle ground, gaining only a few hundred feet, through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century. It ends well short of the head of the valley, and Rimrock Ridge is beyond where it ends.

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp, end of the road
bivy.capacity: The largest camp in the upper valley, big enough to take groups and long used as a staging point for parties crossing Park Creek Pass or coming over Cascade Pass. Still permit-assigned by night.
bivy.water: River and tributary water at the camp, reliable all season and needing treatment like everything else in the drainage.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. Book or claim the nights in the same transaction as the rest of the itinerary; a party walking this far does not want to discover a gap in the middle of it.
bivy.notes: Twenty-three miles from the landing at the very end of the old road, something under four miles past the Flat Creek junction. It is included because it is the upper valley's anchor camp and the obvious fallback if Flat Creek Camp is taken, at the cost of walking past your turning and back. It also marks where the OTHER approaches join: parties come down to here over Park Creek Pass from the Thunder Creek side, and over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road, which reaches the Flat Creek junction in something over thirteen miles. Either is a genuine alternative to the boat, and both are long. No elevation is recorded because no confident figure was found for the camp itself.

bivy.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
bivy.capacity: No established camping and no site count. THERE IS NOTHING UP HERE. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.
bivy.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet north-facing valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
bivy.permit: THE AGENCY CHANGES ON THIS TRAIL, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. That means a free self-issue wilderness permit rather than a paid park permit, no reservation, and Forest Service party-size limits rather than park ones. The park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is NO named park cross-country zone for Flat Creek — this is not an oversight in the record, the zone system simply does not extend here, because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice applies: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury.
bivy.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It stands on the east side of the upper Flat Creek valley, across from the glaciated back side of the crest that the classic traverse walks along, and accounts of that traverse do not mention it — climbers up there are looking the other way. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. Expect brush low down and then open country once the timber releases. Budget four days minimum for a trip that would be an afternoon if a road came anywhere near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than around the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a whole day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window: the valley approach is snow-free long before the head of it is, and the same fire and flood seasons that have been closing camps in this valley can close the trail as well.

bivy.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
bivy.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp
bivy.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
bivy.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.

bivy.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
bivy.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
bivy.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.

bivy.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
bivy.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties
bivy.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
bivy.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.

bivy.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
bivy.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left
bivy.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
bivy.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.

bivy.name: Rampart Lakes basin
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends
bivy.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
bivy.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.

bivy.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
bivy.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
bivy.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.

bivy.name: Park Lakes basin
bivy.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below
bivy.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
bivy.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.

bivy.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
bivy.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer
bivy.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
bivy.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. Elevation is not recorded here because a confident figure could not be established; it sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.

bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites
bivy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.

bivy.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
bivy.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends
bivy.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
bivy.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.

bivy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
bivy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
bivy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
bivy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. No elevation is recorded here because a confident figure could not be sourced; it sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.

bivy.name: Paradise designated winter group camping area
bivy.capacity: Groups larger than 12; where oversized parties are required to go in winter
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit for group camping, arranged in person through Longmire. The area only opens once roughly five feet of snow has accumulated at Paradise, a deeper threshold than the two feet required lower down.
bivy.notes: Relevant mainly to clubs and courses running Tatoosh objectives as a weekend rather than to a two- or three-person rope team. It is the plowed end of the road, so it is the one winter overnight you can reach without a road walk, at the cost of camping in the busiest spot in the park. From here Lane Peak still means dropping to the Stevens Canyon Road and walking east, so it buys convenience of access rather than proximity to the climbs.

bivy.name: Ohanapecosh Campground
bivy.capacity: Roughly 179-188 individual sites when operating
bivy.water: Potable water when open; no hookups
bivy.permit: Developed campground, no wilderness permit. Recreation.gov reservation in season.
bivy.notes: The campground on the southeast corner of the park, reached from the Stevens Canyon Entrance, and it is a long drive up the canyon to the Tatoosh trailheads rather than a short one — a fallback, not a base. bivy.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.

bivy.name: The talus and benches below the north face
bivy.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.

bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.

THE FACE ITSELF is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock. Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.

bivy.name: The Tungsten Creek trail camps below the Boundary Trail junction
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the climb beside the creek, most taking one or two tents, with the better ground in the lower half where the timber is still standing. Nothing developed and no facilities, and you are unlikely to meet anyone.
bivy.water: Tungsten Creek runs alongside for the whole climb and is the dependable supply on this approach, holding into the autumn. THIS IS WHERE YOU FILL FOR THE SUMMIT, because the Boundary Trail crest above the junction runs on tarns and snowmelt and is unreliable by August, and the peak itself carries nothing. Old iron pipe from the mining days is scattered along the trail, which tells you where the workings took their water and not that any of it is usable now. Treat everything.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the easy one: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation and nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Thirtymile. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight — this is heavily used horse country. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer in this dry drainage and the wood is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.notes: This is where a party climbing Wolframite from the Chewuch actually sleeps on the second night, and it matters because the arithmetic of the approach is punishing without it. The Tungsten Creek trail breaks off the Chewuch trail a little past eight miles and climbs steadily for about six more, with the creek on the left and the bulk of Wolframite ahead — so a party that has walked in from Thirtymile is looking at a long day before the climbing even begins. Breaking the climb here rather than pushing to the Boundary Trail junction puts you on running water, in shelter, and with the steep work done in the cool of the morning. It is also the sensible fallback when the ground at the junction is occupied by a horse party, which happens more often than the remoteness suggests. Expect burned forest in stretches, little shade, and blowdown that changes with every windstorm. Late July through September is the working season; snow holds on the north sides of the passes above into July.

bivy.name: The Boundary Trail horse camp east of the Tungsten junction
bivy.capacity: An established site roughly a mile east of the junction with the Tungsten Creek trail, laid out with horse feed in mind, so it takes a stock party comfortably and a walking party easily. One of very few genuinely prepared camps along this stretch of the Boundary Trail.
bivy.water: Seasonal and worth checking rather than assuming. There is water at the site early in the year and it becomes unreliable as the summer goes on, in common with everything on this crest — parties have found streams dry and pools with cracked bottoms along this trail in September. Carry up from Tungsten Creek if you are arriving late in the season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Camp on the existing bare ground. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are the norm here by midsummer.
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for a party climbing Wolframite and then continuing east along the Boundary Trail toward Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Basin, which is the classic way to use this corridor — the summits along it are all short detours off the trail with very little gain, and Wolframite is the first of them. Being a mile east of the junction it sits below the peak's south-east side rather than directly under the west approach, so a party going in and straight back out is better served staying at the mine junction ground or lower on Tungsten Creek. Its real value is that it is prepared, level and used, on a crest where most of the camping is improvised. THE WEST SIDE IS THE ROUTE. From the junction the Boundary Trail is followed roughly a mile west to where it turns south for Apex Pass, and the peak is climbed off-trail to the north-east up gentle open slopes; taken well this is easy scrambling, and taken badly it puts you on short steps of harder rock for no reason. Pick the line from below in good light rather than committing to the first gully you meet.

bivy.name: Apex Pass and the high ground west of Wolframite
bivy.capacity: Open alpine ground at and around the pass with room for a small party or two on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind from wind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and the odd tarn early in the season, and frequently nothing at all by late summer. This is a place you carry water to, not one you collect at. The last dependable source coming up is Tungsten Creek; coming from the Cathedral side it is the lake basins, which are a long way west. A party that has not carried enough will be walking a long way down for it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota, no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at whichever trailhead you used. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this height and the alpine turf is fragile enough that a footprint lasts years, so pitch on gravel or rock.
bivy.notes: The pass is where the Boundary Trail bends south a mile west of the Wolframite approach, and it is the link between this peak and the Cathedral country — Apex Mountain stands immediately above it, Amphitheater and Cathedral Peak are further west, and a party collecting summits along this crest will pass through here whichever direction they are travelling. As a camp it is bought and paid for in water and wind: the position is superb and the ground gives no protection at all. Its argument is position rather than comfort, since from here Wolframite is a short morning to the east and Apex is a short morning above. WHAT IT IS NOT is a substitute for a lower camp on a first night — a party arriving here tired and dry has made the trip harder, not easier. Snow lies on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much longer after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when the crest is worth traversing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights up here are properly cold by then.

bivy.name: Teapot Lake and the Boundary Trail benches toward Bauerman Ridge
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and on the benches either side of the trail, room for a party or two at each. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and long odds against meeting anyone.
bivy.water: Teapot Lake is the dependable one on this stretch and that is precisely why parties camp at it rather than on the ridge — but it is a small standing body and has been found stagnant in a dry year, so treat it properly and take it from an inlet if there is one running. The streams and pools between here and the Wolframite junction go dry through the season and cannot be counted on.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit from whichever trailhead kiosk you started at, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, but there is little to burn and the ground is thin.
bivy.notes: The eastern half of the Wolframite corridor, and the camp for a party crossing between this peak and the Horseshoe Basin country rather than going in and out from the Chewuch. It is roughly fourteen miles of mild, high walking from the Tungsten junction east to Horseshoe Basin, staying largely above seven thousand feet, with Bauerman Ridge, Teapot Dome and Horseshoe Mountain all coming off the trail as short detours in the same way Wolframite does. THIS TRAVERSE IS DECIDED BY WATER AND NOT BY DISTANCE. In a dry September the crest carries almost nothing, and parties have walked it past empty pools and dry streambeds with this lake and the occasional trickle as the only supply — which turns a gentle high walk into a rationing exercise. Plan the days around the sources rather than around the miles, fill at every one, and treat any pool as suspect. The far end of this line is the Iron Gate trailhead above Toats Coulee, whose last six miles of road want high clearance, and whose Horseshoe Basin camps are recorded in the eastern Pasayten file rather than here.
